hero.headline: Beetlejuice musical runs through Saturday at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
hero.teaser: The Broadway hit runs June 2 through June 7 at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall, bringing spooky humor and over-the-top visuals to Palm Beach County.
hero.body:
Beetlejuice the musical has landed at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach. Running June 2 through June 7, the Broadway hit brings its spooky humor, over-the-top visuals, and heartwarming moments to Palm Beach County. Actor Ryan Stajmiger steps into the iconic striped suit to play the mischievous demon beloved from Tim Burton's 1988 film. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a strange and unusual teen, whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is laughing with the audience. Very early in the run, he experienced an unexpected moment when a wig change went awry. I have a wig change on stage that Im wearing two wigs... The second wig came off with the first wig, so I was bald for an entire scene, and I got to play with that a little bit, he explained.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50, and the safest and most secure way to get them is to buy directly at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds receives death threats during Florida gubernatorial campaign, calls for responsible political rhetoric
cards.teaser: Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking publicly about death threats against his life as he campaigns for the Republican nomination in the Aug.
cards.body:
Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary. The Naples Republican, in his third term in Congress, faced one threat on social media last month after re-sharing President Donald Trump's endorsement in the Governor's race. A second person called Donalds' district office making similar threats, saying he was going to blow up the entire office. "Somebody just flat out said they were going to kill me," Donalds told radio host Mark Levin on Friday.

Donalds cited the assassination of conservative Charlie Kirk last year as an example of what happens when opponents are demonized and not treated as human beings. He said that demonizing someone to the point of suggesting they will destroy Florida gives an opening to somebody with real mental health issues to do something dangerous. While Donalds considers himself a free speech absolutist, he stressed the importance of being mindful of language to avoid creating an environment where someone takes it upon themselves to take another's life. Despite the threats, Donalds said the incident strengthened his resolve to work hard to be Florida's next Governor and keep Florida free. He is undeterred and confident in his position in the race to succeed Ron DeSantis.

cards.headline: Rental assistance in Palm Beach County overwhelmed as applications fill in hours
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program receives about 600 applications in the first couple of hours each month, far outweighing the nearly $2 million in available grant funding.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program is overwhelmed with demand, with applications filling within hours of opening each month. Dr. James Green, director of the Community Services Department, said the county receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance monthly and currently has about 800 applications in the queue. Applications typically fill within the first couple of hours they open at the beginning of each month. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked CLOSED due to high demand. The program has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding available. Green urges anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check availability, and for those unable to access the county program, 211 is available 24/7 to connect residents with nonprofits and other assistance programs.

The surge in applications reflects rising costs of living across housing, gas, and food. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Joanne Bromfield, who moved to West Palm Beach from Tampa, switched careers from education to real estate seeking higher income but worries about paying rent almost every day. Green said preventing homelessness depends on everyone and is calling on people with extra housing to partner with the county to help neighbors in need.

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 1 in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties
hero.body:
Starting June 1, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties will need to stop using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen on their lawns and landscaping. The restriction will remain in place through the rainy season and aims to protect local waterways from nutrient-laden runoff that fuels algae blooms.

Jordan Skaggs, who works with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained that the ban is designed to reduce the amount of nutrients washing into waterways during heavy rains. The Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River are among the areas most vulnerable to algae blooms triggered by excess nutrients. These blooms create several problems for aquatic ecosystems. According to Skaggs, "It can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife." When algae blooms reach high concentrations, they can become dangerous. "At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health."

For those concerned about maintaining their landscapes during the ban, there is a practical alternative. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting. Ricketts said, "It can be like a small trash can. That is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape." Composting allows residents to continue caring for their gardens and landscaping without relying on commercial fertilizers that could contribute to water quality problems.

The fertilizer restrictions apply throughout all three counties to both lawns and landscaping. Once the rainy season concludes, residents will be permitted to resume using fertilizers containing phosphorus and nitrogen. The temporary measure represents a community effort to protect the region's sensitive waterways during the months when heavy rainfall increases the risk of nutrient runoff entering local rivers and lagoons.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island erosion threatens to split island in half at Peck Lake
cards.teaser: A state report warns that nearly the entire 11.5-mile coastline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, with the ocean potentially breaking through at Peck Lake and splitting the island.
cards.body:
The 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report found Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breach could turn a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. Among sites at risk is the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, along with wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said there are over 33 threatened and endangered species in those areas.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues to fight erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project, dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field said the town is reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over, noting that about $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment every year. Field warned that if an island breach occurs, repairs could require massive state and federal investment, and if funding for beach renourishment goes away, Florida's coastline will change very quickly.

cards.headline: Florida may ban Fourth of July fireworks across state due to drought
cards.teaser: State leaders are weighing whether to ban fireworks for the Fourth of July's 250th anniversary celebration as drought conditions worsen across Florida.
cards.body:
The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services says this year's drought is even more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was put in place. The entire state of Florida is at least abnormally dry, with areas including Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing a range of moderate to extreme drought conditions. State leaders are weighing whether to ban fireworks for the 250th anniversary of American independence.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning about the possibility of a ban. "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about obviously, potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time," Simpson said in May. Simpson acknowledged the significance of this year's holiday but urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, the store has already seen increased customer activity ahead of the holiday. Bill Murphy of Sky King Fireworks said the store monitors the drought index closely to ensure the ground is saturated enough, but noted there is plenty of rain in the forecast. The Department of Agriculture said a fireworks ban would be a last resort.

cards.headline: Florida voters divided on property tax ballot measure requiring 60% approval
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide this November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption, a proposal drawing mixed reactions in West Palm Beach.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to raise the homestead exemption to roll back property taxes, drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents. The ballot measure requires 60% approval to pass. A similar proposal to raise the homestead exemption failed in 2018. The amount of money cities and counties would lose under the plan is still being calculated, and budget cut locations remain unknown if the measure passes.

Homeowners generally supported the proposal. Brian Edington said he supports it because it benefits people who permanently live in Florida, calling it "a really good idea because it saves the people that really live in Florida, the homeowners." He said he is comfortable with local governments spending less and pointed to his neighborhood's trash services as an example, noting they pick up twice weekly when once a week would be adequate. However, renters expressed skepticism. One resident along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said the savings would not reach them, stating landlords would raise rent on all renters. Another Florida resident argued the system should tie more directly to services people use, saying he should not have to pay for schools when his child is out of school.

cards.headline: Florida Supreme Court adopts AI rules for attorneys after rampant courtroom misuse
cards.teaser: Florida attorneys and self-represented litigants will be required to certify that what they cite in court exists and is accurate starting June 15.
cards.body:
The Florida Supreme Court recently adopted new rules addressing the misuse of artificial intelligence in courtrooms, a growing crisis that has prompted the state's highest court to act. Under the new rules, which take effect June 15, Florida attorneys and self-represented litigants will be required to certify that what they cite in court exists and is accurate. Sanctions for violations could range from a public reprimand to fines and even suspension. Federal Judge William Matthewman, the chief magistrate for the Southern District of Florida, said fake evidence, fabricated facts and bogus case law have become so much of a concern that the situation is unlikely to improve quickly. "Unfortunately, I see it getting worse before it gets better," Matthewman said. "I think the Florida Supreme Court's order will help in Florida, but I unfortunately have seen over the last couple of years that it is growing and growing and growing."

In Polk County, an attorney representing the Polk County School District in an ongoing lawsuit over school bus cameras was recently chastised after a judge discovered fabricated facts and cases that don't exist were filed as part of a motion to dismiss. In his apology to the court, the attorney said he used ChatGPT as a drafting and research aid but admitted "there was no excuse" for his "failure to verify before filing." A spokesperson for the school district said they are reviewing the matter further to determine if the attorney will be eligible for contracted services again in the future.

cards.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration at Palm Beach State College

cards.body:
ChildNet celebrated 35 foster youth and young adults at its annual graduation ceremony at Palm Beach State College in Broward and Palm Beach County. The nonprofit organization supports foster children and young adults through education, adoptions and independent living resources. Among the graduates were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, both of whom lost a parent and turned to ChildNet for support. The organization equipped them with the resources they needed to move forward.

Diaz shared encouragement for others facing similar circumstances, saying to believe you will be big one day and put effort into it, never giving up on school or dreams. Saintfort echoed that sentiment, stating that if you believe you'll make it, then you're going to make it. Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, called the evening "the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet, DCF and especially the kids who have worked so hard." Diaz is already enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College with hopes of becoming a doctor. Saintfort plans to pursue a vocational program to become a plumber.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast shark dive operators fight federal feeding ban they say threatens conservation tourism
hero.body:
A proposed federal law banning shark feeding off Florida's coast has sparked pushback from the state's diving industry, which argues the measure unfairly targets small businesses and nonprofits while ignoring fishing practices. The bill, H.R. 3831, known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, passed the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, though it includes an exception for commercial harvesting. Supporters describe it as a necessary safety measure to reduce encounters between humans and sharks.

Dive operators say the legislation singles out their work, which often includes education, conservation, and structured shark encounters. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, noted that Congress has not requested operators present their data or explain their methods. The industry maintains a key difference between their practices and commercial fishing: operators conduct underwater baiting during dives rather than surface chumming, which they argue is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats. Commercial fishing operations, they contend, can disperse hundreds of gallons of chum at the water's surface, a practice the bill does not address.

The proposal references Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as a model. However, Florida operators and some researchers point to what they consider a cautionary outcome there. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, states that shark diving in Florida maintains a near perfect safety record. Since Hawaii implemented its ban, industry members note that shark incidents have increased and fatalities have occurred. According to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips now results in a shark biting off caught fish.

Campbell has sent a letter to Congress requesting that senators delay action, conduct additional research, and include all stakeholders, both tourism operators and fishing interests, in developing regulations. He emphasized that operators welcome accountability but want an opportunity to present science-based evidence before rules eliminate their businesses. The diving industry argues that shark tourism supports local economies and promotes ocean conservation awareness while serving both recreational and therapeutic purposes for customers. Campbell said operators are not afraid of sharks or being held responsible, but rather want the chance to prove their practices are safe and beneficial before facing elimination.

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 30 in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties to protect waterways
hero.teaser: Residents will have to pump the brakes on using fertilizer on their lawns or landscaping starting June 30 due to a ban on any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen.
hero.body:
Starting June 30, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties will need to stop applying fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen to their lawns and landscaping. The restriction aims to protect the region's waterways during the rainy season, when nutrient-laden runoff can trigger harmful algae blooms.

Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained that the ban targets a specific environmental problem. When fertilizer washes into waterways during heavy rains, it enriches the water with nutrients that fuel algae growth. These blooms can damage sensitive ecosystems like the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River by blocking sunlight from reaching beneficial aquatic plants that fish and wildlife depend on for food and habitat. In some cases, dense algae blooms produce toxins that threaten both human and animal health while degrading overall ecosystem conditions.

The ban will remain in effect to protect water quality during Florida's wet season, but residents still have ways to maintain their gardens and yards. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a practical alternative. According to Ricketts, composting works much like a small trash can and provides an effective method to add nutrients back into landscaping without relying on commercial fertilizers. This approach allows homeowners to recycle organic waste while nourishing their plants naturally.

The restriction represents a significant step toward reducing nutrient pollution in local waterways. By preventing phosphorus and nitrogen-based fertilizers from entering the ecosystem during peak runoff periods, the counties hope to reduce algae bloom frequency and severity. Residents should plan ahead to transition their lawn care practices before the June 30 deadline and explore composting options that can sustain their landscaping throughout the ban period.

cards.headline: Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties face millions in losses from Florida property tax proposal
cards.teaser: A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimated the potential losses from the new property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption.
cards.body:
Martin County could lose $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29 from the property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. St. Lucie County could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Indian River County could lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29. These estimates come from a study by the Florida Association of Counties.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said if there is a cut when it comes to property taxes, there are going to be some real shortfalls, some real challenges and some revenue is going to have to be made up somewhere. Options like finding new revenue and budget cuts are a possibility, Powell said. "We don't know if it will be an increase in sales tax, we don't know if it will be an increase in user fees for other services, we don't know right now," Powell said. The referendum to raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 will be decided by voters in November. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal is "more of a break for the struggling family that is in a $300,000 home and working several jobs to make sure ends meet."

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway in Vero Beach to make way for mixed-use development
cards.teaser: Crews began taking down portions of the Indian River Mall this week to make way for a revitalization project for the shopping center.
cards.body:
Crews began taking down portions of the Indian River Mall this week as part of a revitalization project for the shopping center. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager overseeing the redevelopment, said the first phase involves demolishing the Macy's building and the former Sears location. Neighbors gathered in the mall's parking lot to watch the demolition. Mary Alice Stopyra, a nearby resident, expressed support for the project, saying "I'm really happy they're tearing this down. It's just degraded over time." Mark Manera, also from Vero Beach, described the mall as looking like "the death of a beautiful building" and noted he had watched it decline year after year during his visits over the years.

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a new sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with approximately 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. "They're not going to see a dead mall for the last 12 years that was getting cobwebs," Scarfone said, calling it "a city within a city." He hopes to complete the first phase by 2027, though the team is still working on permitting for the remainder of the project. Manera expressed optimism about the changes, saying "If that brings new life, new jobs, new opportunity, that's wonderful."

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup and Walmart over alleged worms in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections after finding live worms in SpaghettiOs purchased at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee.
cards.body:
Mary Hubbard from Okeechobee County is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart after she and her daughter allegedly found live worms in their SpaghettiOs. According to the complaint, Hubbard discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food. She documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the food product. The incident occurred in June 2024 when Hubbard purchased the SpaghettiOs at the Walmart Supercenter store on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee.

Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications as a result. The lawsuit seeks $50,000 in damages and alleges the companies failed to properly inspect the product. Campbell Soup Co. said the claims lack merit, while Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Stuart lawmaker Toby Overdorf supports property tax proposal as voters prepare for November ballot
cards.teaser: Republican lawmakers, including state Rep. Toby Overdorf from Stuart, contend local governments are taking in too much tax revenue and spending too much.
cards.body:
State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said he supports the property tax referendum heading to voters in November. "This is more of a break for the struggling family that is in a $300,000 home and working several jobs to make sure ends meet," Overdorf said. "I'm happy that we have a proposal out to the voters, they can make a decision with it." The referendum would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, requiring 60% voter approval to pass.

Government officials are working to assess the financial impact of the proposal. A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimated potential revenue losses across the region: Palm Beach County would lose $280 million in 2027-28 and $523 million in 2028-29; Martin County $50 million and $93 million; St. Lucie County $80 million and $140 million; Indian River County $32 million and $57 million; and Okeechobee County $4 million and $7 million. Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said local officials are restricted by state law from endorsing or opposing the referendum but can provide educational information. The savings for homeowners can vary from hundreds to thousands of dollars depending on county, city and home value.

hero.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration in Palm Beach County
hero.teaser: 35 students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth and young adults served by the nonprofit.
hero.body:
Thirty-five young adults marked an important milestone at ChildNet's graduation celebration held at Palm Beach State College. The event honored foster youth and young adults served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit organization. ChildNet provides comprehensive support to foster children and young adults through educational programs, adoption services, and independent living resources designed to help them succeed.

Among those celebrating their achievement were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, two graduates who had experienced the loss of a parent and sought help from ChildNet during difficult times. The organization provided both young adults with the tools and support they needed to overcome their challenges and move forward with their lives. Diaz shared advice for other young people facing similar circumstances, telling them to maintain belief in their future success and commit to their education and personal goals. "Belief that you're going to be big one day and just put effort into it, never give up on school and never give up on dreams," Diaz said. "If you push past with the pain and just keep trying hard," she continued, emphasizing the importance of perseverance through hardship. Saintfort offered his own perspective on achieving success, encouraging others to have confidence in themselves. "Believe that you'll make it, then you're gonna make it," he said.

Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, spoke about the significance of the evening's celebration. He acknowledged the collective effort that made the graduates' success possible, recognizing the dedication of case workers from both ChildNet and the Department of Children and Family Services. Rein emphasized that the graduates themselves deserved the most credit for their accomplishments. "This evening is the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet, DCF and especially the kids who have worked so hard," Rein said.

Both graduates have already mapped out their futures. Diaz has enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College as she pursues her goal of becoming a physician. Saintfort is pursuing a vocational program with plans to become a plumber, pursuing a skilled trade career path. Their stories illustrate ChildNet's impact in supporting vulnerable youth through education and resource provision, helping them transition successfully into adulthood.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway to make room for mixed-use development
cards.teaser: Crews began taking down portions of the Indian River Mall this week as part of a revitalization project for the shopping center in Vero Beach.
cards.body:
Crews this week began demolishing portions of the Indian River Mall to make way for a revitalization project. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager, said crews are working on the first phase by taking down the Macy's and soon the former Sears location. Neighbors expressed support for the demolition. Mary Alice Stopyra said she was happy about the teardown because the mall "has degraded over time." Mark Manera from Vero Beach described the mall as looking "like the death of a beautiful building" and said he witnessed "a steady decline year after year after year" during his visits over the years. Manera said the community needs change and that new development could bring "new life, new jobs, new opportunity."

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center featuring around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. He described the future development as "a city within a city" and said visitors will no longer see "a dead mall for the last 12 years that was getting cobwebs." Scarfone hopes to complete the first phase by 2027, though the team is still working on permitting for the remainder of the project.

cards.headline: Martin County could lose $50 million under property tax referendum going to voters
cards.teaser: Government officials are working to assess the impact of a new property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills.
cards.body:
A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimated potential property tax revenue losses across the Treasure Coast region if a homestead exemption referendum passes. Martin County could lose $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29. St. Lucie County could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Indian River County could lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29. Okeechobee County could lose $4 million in 2027-28 and $7 million in 2028-29.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said if property tax cuts occur, there will be real shortfalls and challenges requiring new revenue elsewhere. He noted that options like finding new revenue and budget cuts are possibilities, though officials do not know whether this will mean an increase in sales tax or user fees for other services. The referendum, which would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, will be decided by voters in November. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the measure provides relief for struggling families in $300,000 homes working multiple jobs.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County faces $80 million loss under property tax exemption proposal
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29 under a property tax reform referendum going to voters in November.
cards.body:
Government officials are working to assess the impact of a new property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimated potential losses for Treasure Coast counties, with St. Lucie County facing an $80 million loss in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. The referendum would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with voters deciding in November.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said that if property taxes are cut, "there's going to be some real shortfalls, some real challenges and some revenue is going to have to be made up somewhere." Powell noted that options like finding new revenue and budget cuts are possible, though he could not specify whether increases would come from sales tax or user fees. Republican lawmakers, including Gov. Ron DeSantis, contend local governments are taking in too much tax revenue and spending too much. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, characterized the proposal as a break for struggling families in homes valued around $300,000.

cards.headline: Indian River County facing $32 million revenue loss under property tax proposal
cards.teaser: Indian River County could lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29 if voters approve a property tax reform referendum in November.
cards.body:
Government officials are working to assess the impact of a property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. According to a study from the Florida Association of Counties, Indian River County faces an estimated $32 million revenue loss in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29. The referendum would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with voters deciding the measure in November. Other affected counties include Palm Beach County, which could lose $280 million in 2027-28 and $523 million in 2028-29, Martin County facing $50 million and $93 million respectively, and St. Lucie County with $80 million and $140 million in potential losses.

The savings for homeowners can vary from hundreds to thousands of dollars depending on the county, city, and assessed home value. Republican lawmakers, including Gov. Ron DeSantis, contend local governments are taking in too much tax revenue and spending too much. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal offers "more of a break for the struggling family that is in a $300,000 home and working several jobs to make sure ends meet." Local officials say potential solutions to revenue shortfalls could include increases in sales tax or user fees, though nothing has been determined.

cards.headline: Florida voters divided on property tax proposal ahead of November vote
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide this November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners, a proposal drawing mixed reactions from residents.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to raise the homestead exemption to roll back property taxes, a proposal drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents. The ballot measure would need 60% approval to pass. A similar proposal to raise the homestead exemption failed in 2018.

Brian Edington said he supports the idea because it benefits people who permanently live in Florida. "I think it's a really good idea because it saves the people that really live in Florida, the homeowners," Edington said. He pointed to his own neighborhood as an example of where cuts could be made, noting that trash services pick it up twice a week when once a week would be adequate. While homeowners were generally supportive of paying less in taxes, renters expressed skepticism. One resident along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said the savings would not reach renters and predicted landlords would raise rents in response.

cards.headline: Glades Day football targeting state championship after playoff run last season
cards.teaser: The Glades Day Gators are working through summer training in Belle Glade with one goal: returning to state championship glory.
cards.body:
The Glades Day Gators are putting in the work this summer in Belle Glade with one goal in mind: a return to state championship glory. The Gators finished last season with a 4-9 record but made a run in the SSAA playoffs, reaching the third round before their season ended. Head coach James Threlkeld said the playoff push offered a valuable lesson for the team. "The way we were able to turn it around in the playoffs, you know, that was a lesson learned," Threlkeld said. "I think, more for our kids, that was just kind of a decision they made, so we're trying to carry over that mindset."

Threlkeld said the summer months are critical for building toward a strong fall campaign. "Getting yourself acclimated to the heat and the humidity is only gonna help us whenever we start camping," Threlkeld said. "You know they have helmets and pads on, you know I think that's a key part." The Gators last won a state title in 2010. Senior Ramsey Rimes said adding another championship would be meaningful for his senior year, while fellow senior Preston Sanford said breaking that streak would mean a lot to the team.

hero.headline: Beetlejuice musical runs through Saturday at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
hero.teaser: The Broadway hit runs June 2 through June 7 at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall, bringing spooky humor and over-the-top visuals to Palm Beach County.
hero.body:
Beetlejuice the musical has landed at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach. Running June 2 through June 7, the Broadway hit brings its spooky humor, over-the-top visuals, and heartwarming moments to Palm Beach County. Actor Ryan Stajmiger steps into the iconic striped suit to play the mischievous demon beloved from Tim Burton's 1988 film. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a strange and unusual teen, whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is laughing with the audience. Very early in the run, he experienced an unexpected moment when a wig change went awry. I have a wig change on stage that Im wearing two wigs... The second wig came off with the first wig, so I was bald for an entire scene, and I got to play with that a little bit, he explained.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50, and the safest and most secure way to get them is to buy directly at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

cards.headline: 80-mile ocean paddle from Bimini to Lake Worth Beach to raise cystic fibrosis funds
cards.body:
More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the open Atlantic Ocean this June as part of the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis. Event founder Travis Suit will lead participants launching from Bimini, Bahamas at midnight on June 13, with paddlers expected to reach Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours on the water. The expedition benefits the Piper's Angels Foundation, which Suit created in honor of his daughter Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

The four-day event begins June 10 with participant arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. Thursday includes a beach cleanup organized by 4Ocean and a community dinner. Friday features a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before the midnight launch. All paddlers must wear U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices, waterproof whistles, and reflective gear. GPS trackers provided by organizers must be worn and kept active throughout. Individual paddlers must raise at least $2,000, while crew members and virtual participants must raise a minimum of $500, with all contributions due by July 31. The public is invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to welcome arriving paddlers.

hero.headline: Byron Donalds calls for Republican unity ahead of Florida primary, declines debates with opponents
hero.teaser: Byron Donalds says Republicans should coalesce behind his gubernatorial campaign more than two months before the August primary, citing his fundraising lead and polling advantage.
hero.body:
Byron Donalds declared Friday that the general election has effectively begun following Jerry Demings' withdrawal from the Democratic primary for Governor due to a prostate cancer diagnosis. The Naples Republican, positioning himself as the clear frontrunner in the Republican race, called for party unity more than two months before the August 18 primary election.

Donalds has raised $81 million and stated he would rather invest those resources in the general election than the primary, given that Democrats now have a presumptive nominee. He emphasized his complete and total endorsement from President Donald Trump and cited polling showing him leading by more than 40 points as evidence of his strength. In his pitch for Republican consolidation, Donalds contrasted his vision with that of his Democratic opponent, saying the differences could not be more stark. "Jolly would end the Florida Dream and transform our state into another Virginia, Illinois, California, or New York," Donalds said. "Millions of people have come to Florida to escape the craziness of blue state governance and they are not going back." He called on Republicans to unite around defending Governor DeSantis's record and keeping Florida free.

Rather than participate in debates with Republican opponents, Donalds announced he would engage voters through alternative means. He argued that all other candidates poll in single digits and that intra-party conflict only benefits Democrats. "At this point, fighting amongst Republicans only helps the Democrats end the Florida Dream we all love and cherish," Donalds said. His campaign instead plans to conduct town halls, community meetings, business roundtables, and door-to-door outreach to communicate his message of conservatism and common sense directly to Florida voters.

His rivals reject this approach. Jay Collins launched The Collins Callout website Friday, challenging Donalds to participate in debates and questioning whether he would "answer the bell, or keeps running." Former House Speaker Paul Renner posted a video to social media making a similar plea, saying both Collins and Donalds were unwilling to debate him. "Floridians deserve to see the differences between the candidates. Stop ducking and let's get on stage," Renner said. Through the end of March, Renner had raised more than $6 million while Collins raised approximately $1.75 million. Updated fundraising reports covering activity through May are due June 10.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds receives death threats during Florida gubernatorial campaign, calls for responsible political rhetoric
cards.teaser: Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking publicly about death threats against his life as he campaigns for the Republican nomination in the Aug.
cards.body:
Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary. The Naples Republican, in his third term in Congress, faced one threat on social media last month after re-sharing President Donald Trump's endorsement in the Governor's race. A second person called Donalds' district office making similar threats, saying he was going to blow up the entire office. "Somebody just flat out said they were going to kill me," Donalds told radio host Mark Levin on Friday.

Donalds cited the assassination of conservative Charlie Kirk last year as an example of what happens when opponents are demonized and not treated as human beings. He said that demonizing someone to the point of suggesting they will destroy Florida gives an opening to somebody with real mental health issues to do something dangerous. While Donalds considers himself a free speech absolutist, he stressed the importance of being mindful of language to avoid creating an environment where someone takes it upon themselves to take another's life. Despite the threats, Donalds said the incident strengthened his resolve to work hard to be Florida's next Governor and keep Florida free. He is undeterred and confident in his position in the race to succeed Ron DeSantis.

cards.headline: Democrat Benjamin Sandlin launches second campaign for Jacksonville House District 12
cards.teaser: Benjamin Sandlin filed for the Jacksonville House race Friday, just three days before qualifying begins Monday, after losing the same seat by 14 points two years ago.
cards.body:
Democrat Benjamin Sandlin is launching a second run in Jacksonville's HD 12, where he lost by 14 points to House Speaker Pro Tempore Wyman Duggan two years ago. The Republican-leaning seat is open because Duggan is term-limited. The 22-year-old candidate filed for the House race Friday, three days before qualifying begins Monday, June 8. After discussions with the Florida Democratic Party, who agreed the seat was too close in 24 to leave uncontested, Sandlin told Florida Politics on Saturday morning it would be a huge missed opportunity to have an extra voice for labor rights, public schools and housing justice in the Legislature. As the sole Democrat in HD 12, Sandlin is likely to advance to the November ballot upon qualifying.

Sandlin had previously filed for the race to succeed Democrat Jimmy Peluso in City Council District 7 but dropped out. The District 7 race remains crowded with six Democrats and a no party affiliation candidate on the ballot. In HD 12, Former Jacksonville City Council President Terrance Freeman is running to succeed Duggan and is well-positioned for his Primary. Through the end of May, Freeman raised more than $167,000 to his campaign account and an additional $506,000 to an affiliated political committee, For the Future We Want, with roughly $390,000 on hand. Freeman was appointed to Jacksonville City Council in 2018 by former Gov. Rick Scott and was elected to an at-large seat twice in 2019 and 2023.

cards.headline: Former Lake County Property Appraiser Carey Baker enters race for Florida Congressional District 11
cards.teaser: Carey Baker is running to succeed retiring U.S. Representative Daniel Webster, setting up a GOP Primary with Lake County Commissioner Anthony Sabatini.
cards.body:
Former Lake County Property Appraiser Carey Baker is running to succeed retiring U.S. Representative Daniel Webster in Congressional District 11. The 63-year-old Eustis resident represented much of the Central Florida district in Florida's Legislature, serving in both the House and Senate, before being elected countywide as a constitutional official. Baker most recently served multiple terms as Property Appraiser but lost re-election in 2024 after filing as a write-in candidate. He was defeated by Republican David Jordan by a 3-to-1 margin in the General Election.

Despite his election loss, Baker demonstrated fundraising prowess that will come in handy in the race for the nomination, raising $233,000 for the campaign. He is poised for a GOP Primary with Lake County Commissioner Anthony Sabatini, who has already run for the seat. After the latest round of Congressional redistricting, Florida's 11th Congressional District includes all of Sumter County, some of west Orange County and most of Lake County. Baker has remained a high-profile Republican leader in Lake County since his election to the Florida House in 2000 before he ascended to the Florida Senate. His father also served the area in the Florida House. CD 11 is likely to be Republican in November, as more than 57% of voters there backed President Donald Trump in the 2024 Presidential Election.

cards.headline: Cuba's Raúl Castro makes first public appearance since U.S. murder charges over 1996 plane downing
cards.teaser: Cuba's former president appeared at his 95th birthday celebration with top officials in Havana, his first public sighting since U.S. indictment for alleged role in downing civilian aircraft.
cards.body:
Raúl Castro, Cuba's low-profile former president and revolutionary guerilla, made his first public appearance since being indicted by the United States for his alleged role in the 1996 downing of two civilian aircraft. State TV broadcast footage of Castro, clad in his olive-green military uniform, entering a packed theater at the Ministry of Interior in Havana on late Friday to a standing ovation, followed by his grandson and bodyguard Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez and Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel. The celebration of Castro's 95th birthday offered Cuba's socialist government an opportunity to close ranks and project defiance as the Trump administration escalates its pressure campaign on the fuel-starved island.

Díaz-Canel delivered an effusive tribute to the "heroism and dignity" displayed by Castro and his late brother Fidel Castro. He praised Raúl Castro, who served as defense minister of Cuba for nearly 50 years, for his "courage and loyalty" that made him a target for the intelligence services of enemies. The Justice Department's indictment unsealed last month accuses Castro of ordering the 1996 shootdown of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles. This marked the steepest escalation since the Trump administration all but cut off Cuba's oil supplies in January, exacerbating the island's long-running problems like blackouts and a public health crisis.

cards.headline: Senator Rick Scott honors father's D-Day service on 82nd anniversary of Normandy invasion
cards.teaser: The Naples Republican and Navy veteran remembered his adopted father who parachuted behind enemy lines during the 1944 operation.
cards.body:
Senator Rick Scott is keeping the memory of World War II alive by honoring his father's service on the 82nd anniversary of D-Day. The Naples Republican and Navy veteran is remembering what many members of the military faced during the famous 1944 World War II military operation, wherein more than 160,000 Allied troops stormed the beaches of Normandy and made first headway in the liberation of German-occupied France. Orba Scott, who raised the Senator, was among those engaged in the operation. As the Senator recounts, his adopted dad parachuted behind enemy lines and selflessly fought for the well-being and freedom of Americans and families across the world.

Sen. Scott acknowledged that his father was blessed enough to return home from battle, but many brave individuals made the last full measure of devotion in defense of freedom and did not return home. As a Navy veteran and the son of an Army veteran, Scott vowed to continue fighting for those who have fought for America. He said he is fighting every day to improve the military, take care of the nation's veterans, and protect the legacy so the next generation knows and appreciates the sacrifices made for their freedoms.

cards.headline: Gatorland opens craft beer bar with exclusive brew from Crooked Can Brewery
cards.teaser: The Orlando park launched the Guzzlin Gator Beverage Barn on Memorial Day Weekend, featuring the Grinnin Gator lager available only at the park.
cards.body:
To celebrate the start of summer, Gatorland opened the Guzzlin' Gator Beverage Barn on Memorial Day Weekend, an outdoor, shaded bar featuring an exclusive craft beer made by Crooked Can Brewery. The Grinnin' Gator lager, a Pale German lager with hints of citrus, can only be found at the park. The beverage barn also serves five other pours, including beers from Orlando's Ivanhoe Park and Orange Blossom breweries and St. Petersburg's 3 Daughters Brewing. The space is located near the Legends of the Swamp show and is designed to give Gatorland guests a place to relax in the heat.

Tim Acheson, Gatorland's Director of Food and Beverage, described the Grinnin' Gator as a "summertime sipper" with citrus notes including grapefruit and orange peel that remind him of Florida. Alan Delahunt, Managing Partner at Crooked Can Brewing Company, explained the brewery chose a pale lager because "we wanted to provide a beer that was kind of a beer for everybody." Acheson is already envisioning expanding the menu with kiddie cocktails and dirty sodas to accommodate families with kids. The Grinnin' Gator is currently served in plastic cups, but Gatorland plans to sell six-packs with decorative cans in the gift shop for guests to take home. Additional beer collaborations are in the works at Gatorland.

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban takes effect June 30 in Martin County to protect St. Lucie River
hero.body:
Starting June 30, residents in Martin, Indian River, and St. Lucie counties will no longer be able to use fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen. The ban applies to all lawn and landscaping fertilizer use and will remain in effect through the rainy season. The restriction is designed to combat a significant environmental problem that affects the region's waterways during months when heavy rainfall increases nutrient runoff.

Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained that the ban serves an important purpose for protecting local water systems. Nutrient-rich runoff from fertilizers can trigger algae blooms in sensitive areas like the Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River. These blooms create multiple problems for the ecosystem. They block sunlight from reaching beneficial aquatic plants that fish and wildlife depend on for food and habitat. In more severe cases, harmful algae blooms can accumulate to densities where they produce toxins that threaten human health, harm wildlife, and damage the overall health of the ecosystem.

For residents concerned about maintaining their gardens and landscapes during the ban, Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an effective alternative. Ricketts described composting as a simple and practical solution that doesn't require complicated equipment or techniques. According to Ricketts, composting can work "like a small trash can" and represents "the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape." This approach allows residents to continue caring for their outdoor spaces while avoiding contributions to nutrient pollution in local waterways.

The three-county fertilizer ban reflects growing concerns about water quality in Florida's coastal regions. By reducing nutrient inputs during the period when rain increases runoff into rivers and lagoons, the ban aims to prevent the conditions that allow algae blooms to develop. Residents who rely on fertilizer for lawn maintenance have several weeks before the June 30 deadline to transition to alternative methods like composting or to use remaining fertilizer supplies responsibly.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue extinguishes nearly 40-acre brush fire in Indiantown
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue put out a brush fire covering nearly 40 acres in Indiantown.
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue extinguished a brush fire in Indiantown that burned nearly 40 acres. The fire was contained by fire rescue crews.

Northbound I-95 traffic near Hobe Sound experienced delays Friday due to a brief law enforcement pursuit. The pursuit affected traffic flow on the interstate.

Stuart unveiled a massive mural to promote ecosystem awareness. The mural was recently completed and put on display in the city.

cards.body: The emergency dispatch center handles calls for Martin County. County officials implemented the improvements to the dispatch facility.

cards.teaser: A Tampa Bay Times column discussed why Dr. Stuart R. Bell is the right president for the University of Florida.
cards.body:
The Tampa Bay Times published a column about Dr. Stuart R. Bell serving as president of the University of Florida. The opinion piece outlined reasons supporting Bell's leadership of the university.

Dr. Bell holds the position of president at the University of Florida. The column appeared in the Tampa Bay Times defending his presidency.

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 30 in St. Lucie, Martin, and Indian River counties
hero.body:
Starting June 30, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties must stop using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen on their lawns and landscaping. The restriction takes effect during the rainy season when heavy rainfall can wash nutrient-rich runoff into local waterways. The ban aims to protect water quality in sensitive ecosystems like the Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River by reducing the nutrients that fuel algae blooms.

According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, the seasonal ban addresses a serious environmental problem. When excess nutrients enter waterways during periods of heavy rain, they can trigger algae blooms that damage aquatic ecosystems. These blooms shade out beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on for survival. In some cases, harmful algae blooms become dense enough to release toxins that threaten human health, wildlife populations and the overall health of the ecosystem.

For residents looking for alternatives during the fertilizer ban, Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting. According to Ricketts, composting provides a practical way to add nutrients back into landscaping without using commercial fertilizers. He suggests using a small trash can as an easy and practical composting method that works well for most homeowners seeking to maintain their gardens and landscapes during the restricted period.

The three-county fertilizer ban represents a coordinated effort to protect regional water systems during the months when rainfall is heaviest. By limiting nutrient runoff at the source, the restriction helps prevent the conditions that lead to harmful algae blooms. Residents who plan ahead and switch to composting methods can maintain healthy landscapes while supporting the water quality improvements the ban is designed to achieve.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce pastor accused of abusing five foster children in her home
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce pastor faces allegations of abusing five foster children who were placed in her care.
cards.body:
Authorities have accused a Fort Pierce pastor of abusing five foster children at her home. The case involves children who were under her care as a foster parent.

Police uncovered alleged child abuse, starvation and filthy conditions inside the pastor's Fort Pierce home. The investigation revealed conditions that prompted law enforcement intervention and removal of the children from the residence.

cards.headline: 18-year-old man accused of shooting 17-year-old girl in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: An 18-year-old man faces charges after allegedly shooting a 17-year-old girl in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police arrested an 18-year-old man accused of shooting a 17-year-old girl. The shooting occurred in Fort Pierce, resulting in the victim sustaining injuries from gunfire.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie to host Juneteenth celebration at MIDFLORIDA Event Center
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie will hold a Juneteenth celebration at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center.

The city of Port St. Lucie will host a Juneteenth celebration at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. The event marks the annual commemoration of the end of slavery in the United States.

The celebration will take place at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center, providing a venue for the community to observe the historical significance of Juneteenth. Port St. Lucie residents will have the opportunity to participate in the city-sponsored event.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County woman accused of stealing $60,000 from bingo hall
cards.teaser: A St. Lucie County woman faces charges for allegedly stealing $60,000 from a bingo hall.

Authorities arrested a St. Lucie County woman accused of stealing $60,000 from a bingo hall. The theft allegedly occurred over a period of time while the woman had access to bingo hall funds.

The woman faces charges related to the alleged theft of the substantial sum from the gaming facility. Law enforcement investigated the missing funds before making the arrest in St. Lucie County.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested after homeowner spots burglary on security camera
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie man was arrested after a homeowner watched a burglary unfold on security camera.
cards.body:
Police arrested a Port St. Lucie man after a homeowner spotted a burglary in progress on their security camera. The homeowner was able to observe the break-in remotely through the camera system and alert authorities.

The real-time surveillance footage allowed law enforcement to respond while the burglary was occurring. Officers apprehended the Port St. Lucie man in connection with the break-in after the homeowner provided information from the security camera.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce port considers new space industry facility
cards.teaser: The Fort Pierce port is looking at developing a new facility to serve the space industry.
cards.body:
The Fort Pierce port is exploring plans for a new space industry facility as part of ongoing development updates. Port officials are eyeing opportunities to expand operations to accommodate space-related businesses and activities.

The potential facility would position Fort Pierce to serve the growing space industry on Florida's east coast. Port leadership is reviewing the proposal as part of broader plans for facility improvements and economic development.

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban takes effect June 30 in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties
hero.body:
Beginning June 30, residents across Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties must stop using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen on their lawns and landscaping. The restriction is designed to protect local waterways during the rainy season when nutrient-rich runoff becomes a significant concern.

According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, the ban targets a critical environmental problem. When fertilizers wash into waterways during heavy rains, they can trigger algae blooms that damage the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. These blooms create serious ecological consequences. "It can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife," Skaggs explained. Beyond blocking sunlight, certain algae blooms at high concentrations produce toxins that threaten human health, wildlife populations and the broader ecosystem.

The rainy season creates ideal conditions for nutrient runoff to reach local waterways, making this the most effective time for the fertilizer restriction. County officials determined that limiting phosphorus and nitrogen during these months would reduce the amount of nutrients entering sensitive aquatic environments. This approach addresses the problem at its source by preventing excess nutrients from washing off treated lawns and landscaping during storms.

For residents concerned about maintaining their landscaping during the ban period, alternatives exist. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a practical solution. "It can be like a small trash can," Ricketts said, noting that composting represents "the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape." This method allows homeowners to continue nourishing their plants and gardens using organic materials rather than commercial fertilizers containing the banned nutrients.
